title: Managing musicians and what the dances paid
summary: Handling difficult players, then pay rates from the Silver Leaf days to the Tuxedo Band.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: They didn't really like it. Some of them used to fuss with me. Some night when they get up, that guy said, you have to get to play and say, I'm hungry. I said, you're hungry? I said, didn't you know you were just coming with the white? And then he didn't know. I said, you need to tell me you can't go about two hours and a half before you're in the mission or three hours or something. He said, no, get out. He said, once more, no slas. He said, no slas. He said, you're in the mission. They get hot with me. But I'm telling you, I made more money from him. I made more money from him. But that's the best time. So everyone knew they weren't going to leave. But you just had to be like that. I didn't mean that. But you got to bluff a little bit sometimes. Sometimes. If you don't care if they could reach you, they'll do you. Yes. I didn't let them go. They felt like smoking it going down straight. I said, what are you doing? No, no. And now, the guy smoked a bed. I said, who are you? Smoking one this thing? I said, where did you get that head? I said, well, they smoked one this thing. I said, you want a sign. You got to be glad you done with these kind of people. I said, you ain't going to smoke one this thing. I said, you ain't going to smoke one. I had a brother, John. He was a good drummer. And he used to get a little lordy sometimes. When he didn't show up, I'd leave for him to get. I'd sing him back a couple of times. He'd been drumming and gone back home. Never come home. He'd never do nothing to show me up. The people would come out there and tell him any kind of stuff. I said, well, I said, he's got a big deal. He's got a big deal. He's got a big deal. He's got a big deal. I was wondering, when you first started out, how much money the musicians made?
What did they pay for dances?
Silver leaf, for instance, way back those days.

When we first started playing, we used to play all around, all the little white dance and everything like that, ten dollars and a half. Three hours. A dollar and a half for men and two hours for the leader. And we played a many again. Ten and a half for the whole band. The whole band. And when we played in the district, we'd be getting down a half a night, but we made two. And I went out on the job, went outside like that. The color dancers used to run from eight to count to the four in the morning. Two and a half a man, three dollars for the manager. And then when we got on up to playing the white school dance and things like that, we used to get five dollars a man. We used to get thirty-six dollars for our band. One dollar over.

That was a tuxedo band. But we was coming up all the time. Yes. You see. So when we stopped playing, we'd get seven, eight dollars on the job paid through. We used to play a key at three and get to the next key for five thirty and get to the next job for now. See, my brothers, way back then they used to be able to make, see when they leave home they'd come back at about eighteen dollars. You see, but none of that other band couldn't do that. They were big at that time, you see. And we'd play at the carnival ball, the big Boston club. We'd get fifteen dollars a man a day to leave in. So then I got twenty-five, down a day. See, I got fifteen. That was well understood. So I said, I carried everything and I used to manage it and keep in mind.
